Dear reporters,

The first brass key went missing on 11 December, eight days before the television people arrived.

Today is the day. The goods train leaves Wickfold station at 6 p.m. sharp, and it will not wait for us. The tower clock blows the four o'clock whistle, and that whistle sends everyone to the loading bay. Loading 2,400 robots takes 90 minutes, the lorries need 15 minutes to the station, and the station master closes the goods yard at 5:45, so we must start at four. On the shop floor nobody may wear a watch near the machines, and the presses are so loud that only the whistle reaches every hall.

My worries:

- On his first visit Mr Brook asked me twice at what time exactly our four o'clock whistle blows. Mr Brook of Tollmann Toys came here on 19 December and again on 22 December, and both times he asked about our train. Mr Brook telephoned me from the Hotel Carrow in Manchester at 08:15 on 21 December. Manchester is five hours from Wickfold by car, and there is no night train.
- In January a new electric clock takes the place of the old tower clock, and Hubert has hardly spoken to me since I told him.
- My daughter Anneliese wants the television crew gone, and she tells them so to their faces. Anneliese spent the night of 20 December in Birmingham, for her interview at the art school.

Please hurry.

::: handwriting
G. Kessler
:::
